pairs.note: THE headline. A stops the nail 0.089m in — one millimetre short of counting as driven — and holds the hammer there, scoring 663.2, the highest of any behaviour collected. B drives the nail all the way home, scoring 601.4. The reward's single favourite trajectory in the entire dataset is one that deliberately never finishes the job.

Both drive the nail fully in. A then thrashes the arm at near-maximum command magnitude (0.90) while keeping the hammer jammed against the finished nail, scoring 552.7. B calmly releases the hammer and retracts (0.56), scoring 414.7. Violent, pointless motion after success is not merely unpenalised — it pays 33% better than tidying up.
The widest inversion in the data — 4.8x. A never drives the nail in (663.2). B drives it all the way into the wall with the gripper (139.5).

Both fully drive the nail into the wall. A strikes it with the hammer (601.4). B pushes it in with the gripper and only afterwards picks the hammer up and holds it against the driven nail (365.7). Identical outcome, 1.6x difference in score, decided entirely by which object touched the nail.

Neither trajectory ever drives the nail in. A parks it at 0.089m (663.2); B parks it at 0.05m (528.6). The closer the arm gets to finishing without actually finishing, the more it is paid — the reward has a smooth gradient that runs right up to the goal and then stops paying for crossing it.

lotteries.justification: C = a certain, clean full success driven home with the hammer (T147, 601.4). The lottery's 'good' branch under the designed reward is A = the run that parks the nail 1mm short and never finishes (T122, 663.2); the other branch B = a full success pushed in by the gripper (T025, 139.5). Indifference is p* = (601.4 - 139.5) / (663.2 - 139.5) = 0.882. I chose p = 0.90, just ABOVE p*, so the reward now prefers the LOTTERY (EV 610.9 vs 601.4) — it gives up a guaranteed driven nail for a 90% chance of a run in which the nail is never driven at all. A user is choosing between a sure thing and a gamble that is 90% likely to leave the job unfinished; they would keep the sure thing. The reward says otherwise, and only barely — which shows how little the act of finishing is actually worth to it.

A different shape: BOTH lottery branches fully drive the nail into the wall, differing only in what the arm does afterwards (A finishes cleanly, 601.4; B thrashes at full magnitude while jammed against the nail, 552.7). So the lottery guarantees the task is completed whichever way the coin falls. C is the reward's favourite trajectory overall — the one that stops 1mm short and never finishes (T122, 663.2). Because C outscores BOTH branches, no indifference point exists in [0,1]: the designed reward prefers the certain non-completion for EVERY value of p. I set p = 0.50 so the two branches are symmetric and the only thing the coin decides is HOW the nail gets driven, never WHETHER — making it as plain as possible that the reward is rejecting a guaranteed success in favour of a guaranteed failure.
